source: Hutchins (1995) How a cockpit remembers its speeds, Cognitive Science 19:265-288
finding: Founding cockpit study. The cockpit system remembers approach speeds through a chain of media: weight-indexed speed card booklet, posted card, spoken call-outs, and speed bugs set on the airspeed indicators. Memory is a property of pilots plus artifacts, not of one head.
numbers: Qualitative case from observation in MD-80 cockpits. Hardware: speed card booklet, 2 airspeed indicators with internal and external bugs. No sample size, no error rates, no statistics; the analysis was started in Nov 1988.
quote: In much of the cockpit's remembering, significant functions are achieved by a person interpreting material symbols
limits: Single aircraft type and airline procedure. Cannot be replicated in the experimental sense; evidence is a worked-through description. The author says memory durations and quality in the pilots' heads are unknown.
agent_relevance: A scaffold's memory can live in checkable external records (cards, posted state, cross-checks) rather than in the model's context alone.

source: Hutchins (1995) How a cockpit remembers its speeds, Cognitive Science 19:265-288
finding: Redundant, cross-checked representations catch errors. The checklist has a challenge/response item 'Flight instruments and bugs'; each pilot compares bug positions on their own indicator against the other pilot's and the speed card. Transposition errors are named as the most frequent reading error, citing Norman and Wickens and Flach, not measured here.
numbers: No error counts. Both crew members verbally confirm bug speeds; bugs set minutes before landing; at least 3 independent representations (card, speech, bug).
limits: Error-frequency claim comes from other literature. No measured detection rates for the cross-check.
agent_relevance: Maps to a guardrail idea: key values stored in several forms and compared, not trusted once.

source: Hollan, Hutchins & Kirsh (2000) Distributed cognition: toward a new foundation for HCI research, ACM TOCHI
finding: Defines cognitive ethnography as event-centered and not one technique: it combines interviewing, surveys, participant observation, video and audio recording. It names the limit of observation: inferences are under-constrained, so findings should suggest ethnographically natural experiments. Proposes a loop of ethnography, experiment, design.
numbers: Examples without statistics: Navy navigation (1980s), cockpit automation, 747-400 autoflight interface, digital airspeed tape. Design claim: all state-of-the-art airspeed tapes (Airbus, McDonnell Douglas, Boeing, Fokker) lost the needle behaviour.
quote: the findings of cognitive ethnography may suggest `ethnographically natural' experiments to enrich our data.
limits: Programmatic paper. It proposes experiments (eye movements on alternative designs) but reports none. The design claims are untested here.
agent_relevance: Video plus observation gives hypotheses, not effect sizes; a scaffold built from ethnographic findings still needs a measured test.

source: Hollan, Hutchins & Kirsh (2000) Distributed cognition: toward a new foundation for HCI research
finding: Two principles: the boundary of the unit of analysis is set by functional relations, not by the skin; and cognition is built from internal and external resources at several time scales. The paper says distributed cognition is a perspective on all cognition, not a special kind.
numbers: 2 principles stated in section 2; 3 process types named. No effect numbers.
quote: Distributed cognition looks for cognitive processes, wherever they may occur, on the basis of the functional relationships of elements that participate together in the same process.
limits: Boundary choice is made by the analyst; no test is given for choosing wrongly. A known weak point of the theory.
agent_relevance: The agent plus its tools and stored state is the natural unit; evaluate the whole loop, not the bare model.

source: Hollan, Hutchins & Kirsh (2000)
finding: Design consequence of ethnography: pilots using needle indicators rarely read airspeed as a number and use needle position in a space of meaningful speeds. A new airspeed tape was designed to keep that salience. The authors admit it needs experimental test.
numbers: No experiment reported. The newest cockpit (Boeing 737-700) renders a literal copy of the old electro-mechanical dial on a screen.
limits: Design inference from observation only; no pilot performance data. The vendor choice to copy the dial is circumstantial support at best.
agent_relevance: Representation format matters: keep forms that match how the user reads, not raw numbers.

source: Hutchins (2013) The cultural ecosystem of human cognition, Philosophical Psychology
finding: Describes instrumented digital cognitive ethnography of a qualified crew in a high-fidelity Boeing 787 simulator. Data streams: multiple HD video recordings, audio, digital pen data, wearable eye tracking on both pilots, simulator data. A few seconds of activity were analysed (reading a chart and a waypoint list).
numbers: One crew, one scenario. Panel image shows 18 distinct scales. Fixations of about 0.5 s and almost 1 s are described for the chart reading. The crew was more than 30 minutes from destination.
limits: Single crew, no inferential statistics, no inter-coder reliability reported. Cases are chosen to illustrate a theory (trajector projection).
agent_relevance: Modern method: synchronised multi-stream recording. For LLMs the analogue is time-aligned trace logging of tool calls, edits and checks.

source: Bender, Hutchins & Medin (2010) Anthropology in cognitive science, Topics in Cognitive Science 2:374-385
finding: Places cognitive ethnography within cognitive anthropology. Notes formal tools that made the field testable: multidimensional scaling and cultural consensus modeling (Romney, Weller & Batchelder 1986), which answers how many informants are enough (Boster 1985).
numbers: Consensus theory cited as the sampling-size method; no numbers reproduced.
limits: Review article. Consensus modeling applies to knowledge questionnaires, not directly to coded video of work.
agent_relevance: Consensus modelling is a possible reliability method for multi-run LLM codings.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Distributed cognition
finding: Secondary summary of tests of the framework: interactivity with cards and tokens aided Bayesian reasoning and cut base-rate neglect (Vallee-Tourangeau et al. 2015); interactivity reduced harm of working-memory depletion on mental arithmetic (2016); evidence on insight problems is mixed (Chuderski et al. 2021).
numbers: No sample sizes or effect sizes on the page.
limits: Tertiary source with verification tags. Primary papers were NOT opened (403 or wrong page). Pointers only.
agent_relevance: Supports external-state aids but shows the effect is task dependent, not universal.

source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action, Cognitive Science 18:513-549
finding: Experimental companion to the programme: Tetris players rotate pieces on screen to learn the fit sooner than by mental rotation. Page returned 403; not read.
numbers: not verified this session
limits: Not opened; do not cite figures.
agent_relevance: Pointer for agent epistemic actions (run code to learn, not to finish).

source: Hutchins (1995) Cognition in the Wild, MIT Press
finding: Founding book: Navy ship navigation as a computation across people and tools. Described second-hand in Hollan et al. 2000: history of navigation in two cultural traditions, tool use, social organisation of work, learning at the organisational level.
numbers: Book not opened. Only described via HHK 2000, which gives no numbers.
limits: Qualitative; no replication in the experimental sense. Evidence quality is that of a single deep case.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Kirsten et al. (2024) Decoding Complexity: Exploring Human-AI Concordance in Qualitative Coding, arXiv 2403.06607
finding: Deductive coding of German interview segments (from an interview study, n=47) with a human codebook. Agreement falls as task complexity rises, for humans and models alike. Human-human kappa: Task A 0.97 (18 codes), B 0.83 (24 codes), C 0.63 (32 codes).
numbers: GPT-4 vs final human codes, zero/one/few-shot kappa. A: 0.97/0.94/0.95. B: 0.75/0.74/0.75. C: 0.56/0.55/0.58. Temperature 0. Segments pre-extracted by two researchers.
limits: Short workshop paper; number of segments not stated in text read. Model-human kappa never above inter-human (ties on Task A zero-shot). German data. GPT 2023-24 models.
agent_relevance: On interpretive coding of observational data, expect the model to match humans on concrete categories and fall behind on latent ones; verify there.

source: Kirsten et al. (2024) Decoding Complexity: Exploring Human-AI Concordance in Qualitative Coding, arXiv 2403.06607
finding: GPT-3.5 Turbo is weaker and more example-sensitive than GPT-4. Few-shot did not raise kappa for GPT-4 but cut formatting errors and off-codebook codes.
numbers: GPT-3.5 kappa zero/one/few-shot: A 0.74/0.78/0.85; B 0.60/0.58/0.56; C 0.43/0.36/0.34. GPT-3.5 invented 47 non-codebook codes in Task B (more than halved with examples); GPT-4 invented 2. GPT-3.5 input cost about 60 times lower.
limits: Examples were synthetic interviews written by GPT-4 and annotated by humans. No significance tests. The authors note the human benchmark is not infallible.
agent_relevance: Closed codebooks need an out-of-codebook guard; weaker models invent labels.

source: Shen et al. (2026) Can Vision-Language Models Analyze Human-Centered Video? arXiv 2609.27327
finding: Maps how HCI researchers annotate video. Of 1,702 CHI 2026 full papers, 125 annotate video. Viewpoints: external scene 56.0% (70), egocentric 37.6% (47), screen recording 11.2% (14). Annotation authority: researcher or expert 44.0% (55), automatic computational 58.4% (73), participant 4.0% (5).
numbers: Corpus 1,702 papers, 125 video-annotating. Taxonomy of five dimensions. Categories overlap, so percentages exceed 100 in sum.
limits: Only CHI 2026, not ethnography broadly. Counts come from the authors' iterative coding.
agent_relevance: Video coding is now routinely machine-assisted in the field this method lives in.

source: Shen et al. (2026) Can Vision-Language Models Analyze Human-Centered Video? arXiv 2609.27327
finding: Benchmark of 15 tasks, 1,459 task instances, one VLM (gemini-3.7-flash), three workflows. VLM alone nearly matches humans; human verification of VLM output beats both.
numbers: Human-normalised score (0=chance, 100=human alone): VLM alone mean 97.0; VLM plus human verification 121.5. VLM alone met or beat humans on 9 of 15 tasks; verification on 11 of 15 and beat VLM alone on 10. Human time 45.0 s per video alone vs 23.0 s verifying (-48.9%). Cost down 31.3% ($5/h labour) to 44.5% ($20/h). VLM alone $1.07 per hour of video.
limits: Two researchers did human annotation, each task split about 50/50 between conditions. One VLM only. Open datasets, not fieldwork recordings. Verification may anchor humans to the model answer.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct test of LLM-assisted video coding. A verify-then-correct step outperforms either alone; copy that design.

source: Shen et al. (2026) Can Vision-Language Models Analyze Human-Centered Video? arXiv 2609.27327
finding: VLM accuracy depends on the phenomenon, not on viewpoint or reasoning horizon. Observable movement, interface events and speech-linked gesture did well; attention and mental-state cues did badly.
numbers: HNS: attentional orientation 17.8; isolated sign recognition 35.4; mistake handling 47.0; interactional dominance 82.9; outcome and breakdown coding 89.6; workflow reconstruction 118.2; co-speech gesture 128.4; communicative intent 134.0; egocentric spatial grounding 93.8 to 178.8. Predictions that viewpoint (RH1) and local-to-global reasoning (RH3) drive accuracy were not supported.
limits: About 100 videos per task (59 for F1-T1); task-level estimates are noisy. Failure analysis: model treated later activity as proof of successful repair.
agent_relevance: Breakdown and repair coding, central to cognitive ethnography, is where the model fails; do not trust unverified labels there.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Redefining qualitative analysis in the AI era: ChatGPT for thematic analysis, arXiv 2309.10771
finding: Interviews with 17 qualitative researchers, then a co-design experiment with 13 of them. Concerns: transparency, verifiability, consistency, accuracy, prompt effort, review cost. A structured prompt framework (task, background, output format as core) moved attitudes from negative to positive.
numbers: N=17 interviews (12 female, 5 male, ages 20-32, median 27), pilot of 4, then 13 experts coding one focus-group transcript with up to 5 own prompts. Outcome is self-reported confidence; no kappa or accuracy.
limits: Small convenience sample recruited via social media. Attitude, not accuracy. No reliability numbers.
agent_relevance: User trust follows traceability of outputs to source text; build evidence-span citations into any coder.

source: Jain et al. (2025/26) Multi-LLM Thematic Analysis with Dual Reliability Metrics, arXiv 2512.20352
finding: Proof of concept: 3 models, 6 runs each, one psychedelic art-therapy transcript. Between-run agreement is high, but it is agreement among model runs, not with humans.
numbers: Cohen kappa across runs: Gemini 2.5 Pro 0.907 (cosine 95.3%), GPT-4o 0.853 (92.6%), Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.842 (92.1%). Consensus themes: 6, 5, 4. Claude kappa range widest (span 0.396).
limits: N=1 transcript, 18 runs, no human comparison. Self-consistency is not validity; shared bias gives consistency.
agent_relevance: Run-to-run agreement is a cheap stability check, not accuracy; pair it with a human or evidence check.

source: Zhang et al. (2023) QualiGPT, arXiv 2310.07061 (numbers from a search snippet of the AHFE version)
finding: Search summary only: GPT-4 kappa 0.57 for inductive coding of Discord data and Fleiss kappa 0.46 for deductive coding; LLM more internally consistent than human coders in the deductive task. The PDF was downloaded but numbers were not confirmed in it.
numbers: Snippet only, not verified in text.
limits: Snippet only; do not rely on exact values.
agent_relevance: Same pattern: moderate kappa, high consistency.

source: Review of LLM-human thematic coding (search snippet; journal-fip.um.ac.id)
finding: A literature review is reported to give human-LLM kappa 0.40 to 0.91, median 0.72, accuracy 77% to 96%, mostly GPT-4.
numbers: Snippet only; not opened.
limits: Not opened. The wide range shows task dependence.
agent_relevance: Plan for 0.4 to 0.9 reliability depending on code type.

source: Park et al. (2023) Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior, arXiv 2304.03442
finding: Simulated agents that observe, store, reflect and plan. Agent interviews tested believability. Removing components lowers it step by step: reflection, planning, memory.
numbers: 100 human evaluators ranked interview answers. TrueSkill mu: full 29.89; no reflection 26.88; no reflection or planning 25.64; crowdworker humans 22.95; no memory, planning, reflection 21.21. Full vs no-memory baseline Cohen d = 8.16. Kruskal-Wallis H(4)=150.29, p<0.001. All pairs significant except crowdworker vs fully ablated.
limits: Believability is rated by crowdworkers, not task accuracy. Agents embellish memories. A simulated society, not an ethnography of real work, but it uses interview-style probing of agents.
agent_relevance: Interviewing the agent exposes which scaffold parts matter; layered memory is a precedent.

source: Cognitive Workspace: Active Memory Management for LLMs (2025), arXiv 2508.13171
finding: Cites Hutchins and Clark as motivation. Active, curated external memory is reported to be reused 54-60% of the time versus 0% for passive RAG, with 17-18% net efficiency gain.
numbers: Reuse: 4-round dialogue 54.52% avg (99 vs 30 operations); 10-round 57.1% with t(18)=69.60, p<0.001; conflict resolution 59.8%; operation ratio about 3.3x. Cohen d reported up to 195.66.
limits: Warning sign: effect sizes of 23 to 196 and a reuse rate defined by the authors with RAG fixed at 0%. Looks like a scripted measure; no downstream accuracy. Not independently replicated.
agent_relevance: Do not treat as evidence that distributed-cognition-style memory improves answers; it shows an overhead trade only.

source: Poquet et al. (2026) Profiling Cognitive Offloading in LLM-mediated Synthesis Writing, arXiv 2606.10434
finding: Uses Salomon's distributed cognition to profile how 97 university students offload to a ChatGPT interface. More offloading goes with lower essay authorship; content of offloading (passive vs active, local vs global) separates groups better than volume.
numbers: N=97; 564 prompts content-coded by one researcher. Volume profiles (k=4): n=51, 22, 17, 7. Silhouette 0.481 for three clusters, 0.412 for four. Essay authorship across volume profiles 5.00, 3.76, 1.16, 0.53 as reported (units as in the table); content profiles k=5 including 12 non-users; p<0.001 on authorship.
limits: One task, one course, single coder for prompt content, arbitrary k-means choices. Correlational: authorship may drive LLM use, not the reverse.
agent_relevance: Passive delegation of comprehension lowers retention; relevant when an agent hands thinking to a person or the reverse.

source: Park, Maciejovsky & Puranam (2025) Thinking with Many Minds, arXiv 2501.02348
finding: Conceptual paper: LLM-simulated deliberation among perspective-holding agents externalises thought (an extended-mind idea). It names over-reliance and cognitive offloading as downsides.
numbers: No experiments in the text I read; no effect sizes.
limits: Theory only; untested.
agent_relevance: Counts as proposal, not evidence.

source: Suchman (1987) Plans and Situated Actions (rival to distributed cognition)
finding: Rival view named in the field: situated action treats plans as resources for action, not controllers; distributed cognition keeps a computational description. Not opened; background without figures.
numbers: none
limits: Not opened. I did not read any direct comparison test of the two views.
agent_relevance: Schema states should guide, not script rigidly.

source: Gap note: no replication of cognitive ethnography studies found
finding: Across all sources opened I found no direct replication or failed replication of the Hutchins cockpit or navigation findings, and no inter-coder reliability study of cognitive-ethnographic video coding. Closest are interactivity experiments (pointers only) and VLM annotation benchmarks.
numbers: Search limits: arXiv API rate limited, Semantic Scholar 429, OpenAlex budget gone, WebSearch budget exhausted after 1 call.
limits: Absence of evidence from a limited search; not proof none exists.
agent_relevance: Evidence level for this subfield is low; treat it as method background.
